summary: Extends OSPF version 3 to support intra-area traffic engineering for IPv6 networks. It extends the OSPFv2 traffic engineering approach by defining a new TLV and several sub-TLVs to carry the needed link information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic planners want to know how busy each road is. This lets routers for newer internet addresses share that kind of information, as the older ones already did.

questions: what is the ospfv3 lsa function code for te
subtitle: How OSPFv3 routers advertise traffic engineering link and address data for IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 traffic engineering carries its data in opaque LSAs and identifies neighbors by IPv4 addresses, which does not fit OSPFv3 and IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5329 defines a new OSPFv3 LSA, the Intra-Area-TE-LSA, that holds one top-level TLV, and adds three sub-TLVs and a Router IPv6 Address TLV to the OSPFv2 TE format.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 routers can flood intra-area traffic engineering information for IPv6 networks, and GMPLS and Diff-Serv MPLS extensions can build on it.

today: RFC 5329 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPFv3 has a flexible way to add new LS types: unknown LS types are flooded properly based on the flooding scope bits in the LS type. This RFC uses that to define the Intra-Area-TE-LSA.

For the TLV definitions it takes RFC 3630 (OSPFv2 traffic engineering) as a base, adds new TLVs and sub-TLVs for IPv6, and clarifies some existing ones for OSPFv3. GMPLS and the Diff-Serv MPLS extensions are based on that OSPFv2 work, so they can be extended to OSPFv3 with the TLVs described here.
sections.plainLanguage: The older routers already shared road-busyness reports. This RFC teaches the newer-address routers to do the same.

sections.title: The Intra-Area-TE-LSA
sections.content:
Unlike OSPFv2 TE, which uses opaque LSAs, OSPFv3 gets a new LS type. The LSA function code is 10, the U-bit is set, and the scope is 01 for area scoping. With the U-bit set, a router MUST flood the LSA within its scope even if it does not recognize the type.

The Link State ID is an arbitrary value used to keep multiple TE LSAs apart and has no topological meaning. The body is nested Type/Length/Value triplets in the same format as OSPFv2 TE. Length counts only the value, in octets. Each TLV is padded to 4-octet alignment, so a 1-octet value has Length 1 plus 3 octets of padding. Unrecognized types are ignored.

An Intra-Area-TE-LSA contains one top-level TLV: type 2 (Link TLV) or type 3 (Router IPv6 Address TLV).
sections.plainLanguage: It is a new kind of note that routers pass around inside one neighborhood, even routers that do not understand it. Each note holds one labeled item.

sections.title: Router IPv6 Address TLV
sections.content:
This TLV advertises a stable IPv6 address that SHOULD be reachable whenever there is connectivity to the router. It has type 3, length 16, and a 16-octet address as its value.

A link-local address MUST NOT be used. The TLV MUST appear in exactly one Traffic Engineering LSA originated by an OSPFv3 router that supports the TE extensions, and only one top-level TLV may be in an LSA.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the router's permanent home address, one that people can always use to reach it.

sections.title: Link TLV and Its Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Link TLV describes one link using sub-TLVs from OSPFv2 TE. All of them apply to OSPFv3 except Link ID, which relies on OSPFv2's way of naming the Designated Router. OSPFv3 always identifies neighbors by Router ID, and the IPv4 interface address is unknown to it. The Link ID sub-TLV SHOULD NOT be sent and MUST be ignored on receipt.

Three sub-TLVs are new:

  • 18 Neighbor ID, 8 octets: the Neighbor Interface ID and Neighbor Router ID. It is mandatory and MUST appear exactly once in a Link TLV.
  • 19 Local Interface IPv6 Address, 16N octets: the interface addresses for the link. Link-local addresses MUST NOT be included.
  • 20 Remote Interface IPv6 Address, 16N octets: the neighbor's interface addresses. With the local one it tells parallel links apart. On multi-access links it MAY be set to :: or omitted.

The other sub-TLVs SHOULD NOT occur more than once; repeats after the first are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each road report names who is at the other end and which addresses sit on each side, so routers can tell two roads between the same towns apart.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
Management is typically SNMP based, using objects from the OSPFv3 MIB, and an implementation SHOULD provide hooks for them. Two MIB variables were added for TE. ospfv3AreaTEEnabled says whether TE advertisement is enabled for an area, default FALSE. ospfv3IfTEDisabled says whether it is disabled on an interface, default FALSE, and applies only when the area setting is TRUE.

The RFC says the function creates no new security issues. The security considerations of base OSPFv3 and OSPFv2 TE apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators get on and off switches for sharing these reports, and nothing about it makes the network less safe than before.
